articleHtml:
Diagnosing Headphone Driver Rattle, Parasitic Buzz, and Harmonic Distortion

A buzzing, rattling, or clicking sound in one ear of your headphones during bass-heavy music is one of the most frustrating acoustic defects. Whether you own high-end planar magnetic audiophile open-backs, studio dynamic monitors, or active noise-cancelling travel headphones, isolating the mechanical cause requires systematic frequency sweeps.

Diagnostic Method: Continuous Sine Sweep vs. Impulse Testing

Pure sine waves excite singular acoustic frequencies without harmonic masking. A slow continuous logarithmic sweep from 10 Hz to 300 Hz reveals structural resonances, loose hair fibers on the diaphragm, and voice-coil rubbing that remain hidden during complex music playback.

1. Primary Mechanical Causes of Headphone Rattle

The "Stray Hair" Effect: By far the most common cause of buzz in open-back dynamic headphones (e.g., Sennheiser HD600/HD650 series). A single short strand of human hair passes through the dust mesh and rests lightly against the ultra-thin mylar diaphragm. When low-frequency sub-bass waves displace the driver, the diaphragm slaps against the hair strand, producing an unmistakable buzzing noise.

Voice Coil Rubbing (Eccentric Alignment): If headphones are dropped or driven beyond their maximum excursion limits, the cylindrical voice coil former can become slightly warped or unseated from the magnetic gap. As the coil moves in and out, it physically contacts the pole piece, creating a harsh metallic rubbing friction.

Diaphragm Crinkling or Delamination: In planar magnetic headphones (e.g., Hifiman, Audeze), the etched aluminum voice coil traces bonded to the ultra-thin planar substrate can experience partial adhesive separation. When energized, the loose trace flutters independently of the membrane.

Loose Chassis Screws or Cable Jacks: The plastic baffle plate, headband gimbals, or detachable 3.5mm input socket can vibrate against the outer shell at specific resonant frequencies (often 120–250 Hz).

2. Step-by-Step Acoustic Inspection Protocol

  1. Set Safe Baseline Volume: Start at moderate listening volume (~65–70 dBA). Never conduct sub-bass frequency sweeps at maximum amplifier gain, as low frequencies below 30 Hz carry massive electrical energy and can blow headphone voice coils.
  2. Run Slow Low-Frequency Sweep (20 Hz → 120 Hz): Listen carefully to each channel individually. Normal playback produces a smooth, clean, continuous tone that rises in pitch. Any buzzing, rattling, or crackling indicates a localized mechanical anomaly.
  3. Hold Resonance Frequency: Once a rattle occurs (e.g., at 48 Hz), pause the sweep and sustain that exact tone. Gently press on different parts of the outer headphone cup, ear-pad ring, and cable entry. If the rattle disappears when pressing the cup, the issue is housing resonance rather than a broken driver.
  4. Inspect Diaphragm with Backlight: Remove the ear cushions and shine a bright penlight at an angle through the driver mesh. Carefully check for tiny hairs or foreign dust particles lodged across the transparent diaphragm dome.
Hearing Safety Warning: Sub-bass frequencies (10–30 Hz) are often felt rather than heard due to human ear threshold curves (Fletcher-Munson). Do not turn volume up to make inaudible sub-bass loud; doing so can cause permanent inner-ear acoustic trauma when higher frequencies occur.
